:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int \dfrac{1}{1+2x}\textrm{d}x},$ writing your final answer as a single function.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=1+2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+2x}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C = \dfrac 1 2\ln K$ for another arbitrary constant $K > 0,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K\cdot |1+2x|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1+2x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{1+2x}\textrm{d}x  = \dfrac 1 2 \ln \left(K |1+2x|\right).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=3x+4.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{5}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|u|+C \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}K$ for another arbitrary positive constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+C & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}K \\  & =\frac{5}{3}(\operatorname{ln}|3x+4|+\operatorname{ln}K) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}(K|3x+4|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{5}{3x+4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{ln}(K|3x+4|).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=2x+3.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+C & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|2x+3|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|2x+3|).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{4}{5x+3}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=5x+3.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{5x+3}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{5x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+3|+C & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+3|+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{4}{5}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5x+3|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5x+3|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{4}{5x+3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5x+3|).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{3}{1-4x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=1-4x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{1-4x}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-4x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-4x|+C & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-4x|-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|1-4x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1-4x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{3}{1-4x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|1-4x|).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{7-x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=7-x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{7-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|7-x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|7-x|+C & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|7-x|-\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡|7-x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|7-x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{7-x}\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|7-x|).
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=5-2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|).
$$
